newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Waigel wants deal to defuse Bundesbank row.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Waigel wants deal to defuse Bundesbank row.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, eager to defuse a row with the Bundesbank, said on Monday he hoped to reach agreement with the powerful central bank on his controversial plan to revalue its assets.

But he said the government would not retreat from the plan to raise billions of marks to help its bid to join Europe's single currency simply by assigning higher values to Germany's undervalued gold and currency reserves.

"We will discuss this with the Bundesbank," Waigel told reporters, adding that the dispute centred on the question of whether to revalue the reserves in 1997 or 1998. "We will try to do this in mutual agreement."
It was a small but potentially important concession from Waigel that followed heavy criticism of his plan to retire old debt with the injection of funds from the Bundesbank.
The conciliatory sounds from Waigel came amid growing worries about plans for the single euro currency.
The electoral victory of France's left on Sunday raised fears in Germany that Socialist demands would derail Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU).

Despite Waigel's offer to negotiate, Bundesbank leaders stepped up their campaign against Bonn's grab for the gold and criticism from newspaper editorials and opposition parties poured down on the beleaguered finance minister.
The government was also deeply divided on Monday over Waigel's plans to fill gaping budget holes but Waigel said there was no danger the centre-right coalition would collapse.
The two main opposition parties, the Social Democrats and the Greens, launched a united bid to call for Waigel's dismissal through a parliamentary vote.
Although Waigel said he was seeking agreement with the Bundesbank, he said he would proceed with Bonn's plan to change the central bank law even without its assent.
Asset revaluation in 1997 could help Germany meet the criteria to qualify for EMU.
Waigel said he believed the Bundesbank, which has expressed its opposition to the proposed accounting changes this year, would be willing to accept revaluation of its assets in 1998.
The plan has led to a remarkably public fight between Chancellor Helmut Kohl and Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer.
Kohl rejected claims by central bank officials who have said the plan to revalue the gold and currency reserves was an infringement on its indepedence.

"Let me state here, clearly and categorically: in no way does the revaluation of the Bundesbank reserves amount to an infringement of the independence of the Bundesbank," Kohl said at an economic conference in Switzerland.
He added, nevertheless, that he was ready for reasonable talks with central bank leaders.

The central bank is not in principle opposed to revaluing its gold reserves but insists that the process should not take place until 1999, or at least not before the decision as to who will participate in monetary union, in May 1998.
The Bundesbank has some 95 million ounces of gold in its reserves, valued at 13.7 billion marks ($8 billion) versus a current market value of more than 55 billion marks.
The Maastricht Treaty calls on countries to keep their budget deficits at or below three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and debt levels at or below 60 percent of GDP.

A trio of Bundesbank council members, speaking in the western German city of Mainz, lambasted the government for seeking to revalue German gold and currency reserves to help it meet these EMU criteria.
Council member Edgar Meister said the monetary union project might enter rougher waters in the weeks and months ahead and Germany must not lose its role as guardian of monetary stability.
Meister added that the French election outcome had changed the environment for EMU and it might become clear in the next few weeks whether the euro would be a stable currency.
Another Bundesbank council member, Hans-Juergen Koebnick, said he did not think European monetary union would be postponed but he thought a delay would be considered.
Speaking at the same event, Bundesbank vice president Johann Wilhelm Gaddum said there was no change in the bank's position since it objected to Bonn's grab for gold last week.
